questions.stem:
A volunteer clinician at a rural health post in Cameroon sees a 22-year-old woman with a painful, nonred swelling of her wrist that appeared 3 days ago, after a similar swelling of her eyelid last month resolved. She also describes the feeling of something moving across her eye. The clinician suspects a fly-borne filarial worm and wants to confirm it with a blood test.

Which specimen is most likely to show the diagnostic form?
choices: Blood smear collected around midday
Blood smear collected at about midnight
Skin snip biopsy placed in saline
Stool ova and parasite examination
Urine collected at midday for eggs

explain.html:
Filarial worms are diagnosed by finding microfilariae where and when they circulate, and that differs by species. Loa loa, transmitted by Chrysops flies in West and Central Africa, has adults that move through subcutaneous tissue, causing painless, nonred Calabar swellings of the limbs or eyelid and sometimes a worm crossing the eye. It releases microfilariae into the blood during the day.

This woman in Cameroon has migrating swellings of the wrist and eyelid and the sensation of something moving across her eye, so the test is a blood smear collected around midday, which shows the microfilaria as the diagnostic form. An adult removed from the eye also confirms it. Wuchereria and Brugia appear in blood at night, and Onchocerca microfilariae are found in the skin, which is why timing and specimen matter.
explain.table:
FilariaVectorAdultsMicrofilariae
Wuchereria, BrugiaMosquitoLymphaticsBlood at night
Loa loaChrysops flySubcutaneous, movingBlood during the day
OnchocercaBlack flySkin nodulesSkin
why: Nighttime periodicity belongs to Wuchereria and Brugia, not Loa loa.
A skin snip finds Onchocerca, whose microfilariae live in the skin.
Filarial worms do not release eggs into the stool.
Eggs in midday urine are the test for urinary schistosomiasis.
explain.takeaway: Loa loa microfilariae circulate in the blood during the day, so diagnosis uses a midday blood smear; Wuchereria and Brugia need a night smear and Onchocerca a skin snip.
explain.topic: Loa loa: collecting the diagnostic specimen
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Identify Loa loa from its presentation and choose the diagnostic test based on when and where its life cycle stage is found.

rows.why: Nighttime periodicity belongs to Wuchereria and Brugia, not Loa loa.
rows.if_right: progressive leg lymphedema after mosquito exposure (lymphatic filariasis)

rows.why: A skin snip finds Onchocerca, whose microfilariae live in the skin.
rows.if_right: intense itching, skin nodules and eye scarring near a fast-flowing river

rows.why: Filarial worms do not release eggs into the stool.
rows.if_right: an intestinal helminth whose eggs pass in feces, such as Ascaris

rows.why: Eggs in midday urine are the test for urinary schistosomiasis.
rows.if_right: painless hematuria after swimming in Lake Victoria

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old woman from Hawaii who is an avid vegetable gardener is brought to the emergency department while visiting family, with 2 days of fever, worsening headache, stiff neck, tingling of her legs, and vomiting. Leukocyte count is 15,600/microL with 13% eosinophils. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a pleocytosis with 17% eosinophils (normal 0), slightly elevated protein, and normal glucose. A resident asks whether stool examination will identify the worm.

Which of the following best explains why stool examination is not helpful?
choices: The worm lays its eggs on the perianal skin at night
The organism is a protozoan that lives only in the bloodstream
Eggs are shed only intermittently, so three separate samples are needed
Larvae reach the brain and die without maturing to egg-laying adults
Adult worms in the lungs release their eggs into sputum

explain.html:
Eosinophilic meningitis is meningitis with a CSF eosinophilic pleocytosis (more than 10% eosinophils; normal is zero). In a person from Hawaii, the classic cause is Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm, and gardening matters because snails and slugs on vegetables carry the larvae.

Humans are accidental hosts. Ingested larvae travel to the CNS, get stuck and die, triggering eosinophilic inflammation, and they never become egg-laying adults in the human gut, so stool studies cannot find them. This avid gardener from Hawaii has fever, headache, stiff neck, paresthesias, 13% blood eosinophils and 17% CSF eosinophils with normal glucose. Treatment is supportive, and most cases are self-limited.
why: Perianal egg laying at night is pinworm, which causes itching, not meningitis.
Angiostrongylus is a nematode, not a blood protozoan.
Intermittent shedding needing three samples applies to Strongyloides, which does have intestinal adults.
Eggs in sputum are a feature of the lung fluke, not of a worm stuck in the CNS.
explain.takeaway: Humans are accidental hosts of Angiostrongylus; larvae die in the CNS and cause eosinophilic meningitis, and stool studies are not useful because no adults form in the gut.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Diagnose eosinophilic meningitis, name its helminth cause from the exposure history, and explain why stool studies do not help.

rows.why: Perianal egg laying at night is pinworm, which causes itching, not meningitis.
rows.if_right: a child with nocturnal perianal itching and a positive scotch tape test

rows.why: Angiostrongylus is a nematode, not a blood protozoan.
rows.if_right: a protozoan seen inside red cells on a blood smear

rows.why: Intermittent shedding needing three samples applies to Strongyloides, which does have intestinal adults.
rows.if_right: chronic larva currens and eosinophilia with one negative stool exam

rows.why: Eggs in sputum are a feature of the lung fluke, not of a worm stuck in the CNS.
rows.if_right: chronic cough and hemoptysis after eating raw freshwater crab

questions.stem:
A 20-year-old woman who recently immigrated from Tanzania is referred for several weeks of painless hematuria. She grew up swimming and washing clothes in Lake Victoria. Laboratory studies show:

[[labs 0]]

Microscopy of a urine specimen shows large eggs with a terminal spine.

How did she most likely acquire this infection?
choices: Swallowing eggs in lake water
Eating raw aquatic vegetation such as watercress
Eating undercooked fish from the lake
Bites of mosquitoes breeding near the lake
Cercariae from snails penetrating her skin

explain.html:
Trematode (fluke) life cycles always involve fresh water and snails. In schistosomiasis, eggs passed by people hatch in fresh water, the larvae infect snails, and the snails release cercariae. The cercariae penetrate intact skin during swimming, bathing or washing and mature into adult blood flukes that live in veins.

This woman from Tanzania who swam and washed clothes in Lake Victoria has painless hematuria, eosinophilia, anemia and large eggs with a terminal spine in urine, which is urinary schistosomiasis acquired through her skin in the lake. Diagnosis is eggs in the specimen, treatment is praziquantel, and untreated chronic disease can lead to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
why: Schistosoma eggs hatch in water and infect snails; they are not the infective form for people.
Raw aquatic vegetation such as watercress transmits plant-borne flukes, not Schistosoma.
Undercooked freshwater fish transmits the fish tapeworm and some liver flukes.
Mosquitoes transmit lymphatic filariasis, which causes lymphedema, not hematuria.
explain.takeaway: Schistosoma is acquired when cercariae released by freshwater snails penetrate the skin; urinary disease shows eggs in urine with hematuria and can lead to bladder squamous cell carcinoma.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Identify urinary schistosomiasis, its mode of infection, diagnostic finding and long-term consequence.

rows.why: Schistosoma eggs hatch in water and infect snails; they are not the infective form for people.
rows.if_right: an organism acquired by swallowing eggs in contaminated water or food

rows.why: Raw aquatic vegetation such as watercress transmits plant-borne flukes, not Schistosoma.
rows.if_right: a liver fluke infection after eating raw watercress

rows.why: Undercooked freshwater fish transmits the fish tapeworm and some liver flukes.
rows.if_right: megaloblastic anemia or biliary disease after eating raw lake fish

rows.why: Mosquitoes transmit lymphatic filariasis, which causes lymphedema, not hematuria.
rows.if_right: leg lymphedema with microfilariae on a night blood smear

labs: More than 180 per high-power field (0 to 2)

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 1 day of severe right eye pain, light sensitivity, and blurred vision. He wore his soft contact lenses far longer than recommended, and after running out of lens solution he has been rinsing them in tap water. He recalls no injury. Examination shows a corneal ulcer, and the pain seems out of proportion to the findings.

Which of the following is the best way to confirm the cause?
choices: PCR of corneal scrapings
Stool antigen testing
Blood smear collected at midday
Cerebrospinal fluid wet mount
Serum antibody testing after 6 weeks

explain.html:
Free-living amebae live in water and soil and cause disease when they reach a vulnerable site. Acanthamoeba is ubiquitous in water and encysts in harsh conditions, so it survives in tap water and contact lens cases and enters through the eye. Overlong wear of contact lenses and rinsing them in tap water are the classic risks for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

This man wore soft lenses far too long, cleaned them with tap water, and now has severe eye pain, photophobia, blurred vision and a corneal ulcer. The diagnosis is made directly from the eye, by PCR or identifying the organism in corneal scrapings or biopsy. In immunocompromised patients the same organism can cause granulomatous amebic encephalitis, while lake-swimming meningoencephalitis points instead to Naegleria.
why: Acanthamoeba keratitis is not an intestinal infection, so a stool antigen test does not help.
A midday blood smear is the test for Loa loa microfilariae.
A CSF wet mount finds Naegleria in meningoencephalitis, not a corneal infection.
Serology after 6 weeks is used for schistosomiasis, not amebic keratitis.
explain.takeaway: Acanthamoeba keratitis, seen in contact lens wearers who rinse lenses in tap water, is confirmed by PCR or identification of the organism in corneal scrapings.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Diagnose Acanthamoeba keratitis, explain how it is acquired, and choose the confirmatory test.

rows.why: Acanthamoeba keratitis is not an intestinal infection, so a stool antigen test does not help.
rows.if_right: an intestinal protozoan causing diarrhea, such as Giardia or Cryptosporidium

rows.why: A midday blood smear is the test for Loa loa microfilariae.
rows.if_right: Calabar swellings and a worm crossing the eye in a Central African resident

rows.why: A CSF wet mount finds Naegleria in meningoencephalitis, not a corneal infection.
rows.if_right: fever, stiff neck and seizures days after swimming in a warm lake

rows.why: Serology after 6 weeks is used for schistosomiasis, not amebic keratitis.
rows.if_right: hematuria with eosinophilia months after freshwater exposure in Africa

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man comes to the clinic 3 months after returning from a long trek in rural East Africa, where he ate meals prepared by local families. Shortly after he got home he had a week of wheezing and dry cough with transient patchy infiltrates on chest x-ray, though he has never had asthma. Now he has upper abdominal discomfort and nausea, and yesterday he passed a pale, smooth, round worm about 25 cm long. Eosinophils are 18% (1 to 4). Stool examination shows thick-shelled eggs with a bumpy outer coat.

Which other nematode passes through the lungs on its way to the intestine but enters the body by a different route?
choices: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm)
Trichuris trichiura
Strongyloides stercoralis
Taenia saginata
Trichinella spiralis

explain.html:
Several intestinal nematodes pass through the lungs before settling in the gut, and the lung passage causes Loeffler syndrome: wheeze, dry cough and transient infiltrates with eosinophilia. They differ in how they get in. Ascaris lumbricoides enters as swallowed eggs, and its larvae travel GUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT. Strongyloides and the hookworms enter as larvae that penetrate the skin, so their route is SKIN, LUNGS, GUT.

This trekker ate food prepared by local families, had an "asthma" episode with transient infiltrates soon after returning, and now passed a 25-cm round worm with mammillated eggs in the stool and 18% eosinophils, which is Ascaris. The nematode that shares the lung passage but enters through the skin is Strongyloides. Worms that are swallowed and stay in the gut, or that head to muscle, have no lung phase.
explain.table:
OrganismEntryRoute
AscarisSwallowed eggsGUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT
Strongyloides, hookwormLarvae through skinSKIN, LUNGS, GUT
Enterobius, TrichurisSwallowed eggsGut only, no lung phase
TrichinellaLarvae in meatGut to striated muscle
Taenia saginataLarvae in beefGut only (cestode)
why: Pinworm eggs are swallowed and hatch directly in the gut, with no lung phase.
Whipworm eggs are swallowed and the adults live in the large intestine without lung migration.
Taenia saginata is a cestode acquired from beef larvae, with no lung phase.
Trichinella larvae go from the gut to striated muscle, not through the lungs to the intestine.
explain.takeaway: Ascaris (GUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT) and Strongyloides or hookworm (SKIN, LUNGS, GUT) all pass through the lungs and can cause Loeffler syndrome, but Ascaris is swallowed while the others penetrate skin.
explain.topic: Helminth migration through the lungs: shared pathways
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Use a returning traveler's history, eosinophilia and the worm passed to identify an intestinal nematode and explain its lung phase.

rows.why: Pinworm eggs are swallowed and hatch directly in the gut, with no lung phase.
rows.if_right: a nematode causing nocturnal perianal itching with no respiratory illness

rows.why: Whipworm eggs are swallowed and the adults live in the large intestine without lung migration.
rows.if_right: bloody diarrhea and rectal prolapse with plugged-end eggs

rows.why: Taenia saginata is a cestode acquired from beef larvae, with no lung phase.
rows.if_right: flat proglottids in the stool after eating undercooked beef

rows.why: Trichinella larvae go from the gut to striated muscle, not through the lungs to the intestine.
rows.if_right: fever, myalgia and periorbital edema after eating rare bear meat

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old man from the Andes of Peru, who grew up on a farm with sheep, pigs, and working dogs, has had 2 years of slowly increasing right upper quadrant fullness and now mild scleral icterus. CT shows a large liver cyst containing smaller daughter cysts, and serology confirms a cestode infection. His wife and adult children, who live with him in the United States, ask whether they could catch the infection from him.

Which of the following is the most accurate response?
choices: Yes, his stool contains eggs that can be ingested by close contacts
Yes, the cyst releases larvae into his blood that biting insects can spread
No, humans are incidental hosts with no adult worm to shed eggs
No, only pork eaten by the family could transmit this organism
Yes, the infection spreads through respiratory droplets from lung cysts

explain.html:
In Echinococcus granulosus, the adult tapeworm lives in the dog intestine, and the dog passes the eggs in its feces. Sheep, and incidentally humans, ingest the eggs and develop hydatid cysts in the liver or lung. Humans are incidental, dead-end hosts: no adult worm develops in a person, so a patient sheds no eggs.

This man raised on a farm with sheep and working dogs has a slowly enlarging liver cyst with daughter cysts, mild icterus and positive serology. He cannot infect his family; anyone in the family who is infected acquired it from the same dog exposure. The one acute danger to remember is that abdominal trauma can rupture the cyst and cause anaphylaxis.
why: Humans with hydatid disease shed no eggs, so stool contacts are not at risk.
Echinococcus is not spread by insects, and the cyst does not release transmissible larvae into the blood.
Pork transmits Taenia solium larvae (taeniasis), not Echinococcus, and humans with hydatid disease are not infectious either way.
Hydatid cysts are not spread by respiratory droplets.
explain.takeaway: Humans are dead-end hosts for Echinococcus: they carry only the hydatid cyst and cannot pass the infection to others, because only dogs harbor the egg-laying adult.
explain.topic: Echinococcus: transmission risk to household contacts
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain how hydatid disease is acquired, how it is diagnosed, and why an infected person cannot transmit it.

rows.why: Humans with hydatid disease shed no eggs, so stool contacts are not at risk.
rows.if_right: an intestinal tapeworm carrier, such as a person with Taenia solium taeniasis

rows.why: Echinococcus is not spread by insects, and the cyst does not release transmissible larvae into the blood.
rows.if_right: a filarial worm whose microfilariae in blood are taken up by biting flies or mosquitoes

rows.why: Pork transmits Taenia solium larvae (taeniasis), not Echinococcus, and humans with hydatid disease are not infectious either way.
rows.if_right: a family that shares undercooked pork containing cysticerci

rows.why: Hydatid cysts are not spread by respiratory droplets.
rows.if_right: a respiratory pathogen such as tuberculosis in a lung cavity

questions.stem:
A public health officer investigates an outbreak of diarrhea in several towns. All patients ate the same bagged salad mix containing imported greens. Illness is watery and nonbloody, lasting a week or more with fatigue and little fever. Routine bacterial cultures are negative. An acid-fast stain of stool shows oocysts 8 to 10 micrometers in diameter. A colleague suggests the organism is Cryptosporidium, which is also acid-fast.

Which pair of features best distinguishes the organism in this outbreak from Cryptosporidium?
choices: Smaller oocysts and treatment with nitazoxanide
Larger oocysts and treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Oocysts that resist chlorine and spread in swimming pools
Tiny spores that are fungi and treatment with albendazole
Flagellated trophozoites on wet mount and treatment with tinidazole

explain.html:
Cyclospora and Cryptosporidium are both acid-fast coccidian protozoa that cause watery, nonbloody diarrhea, so the stain alone does not separate them. Size and treatment do. Cryptosporidium oocysts are smaller (4 to 7 micrometers), resist chlorination and spread in swimming pools, and nitazoxanide is used mainly in immunocompromised hosts.

Cyclospora oocysts are larger, 8 to 10 micrometers, and arrive on fresh produce such as lettuce, herbs and berries; diarrhea can be prolonged, and treatment is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. This outbreak traced to a bagged salad mix of imported greens, with subacute nonbloody diarrhea, little fever and 8 to 10 micrometer acid-fast oocysts, is Cyclospora.
explain.table:
FeatureCyclosporaCryptosporidium
Oocyst size8 to 10 micrometers4 to 7 micrometers
Acid-fastYesYes
Typical sourceFresh produce (lettuce, herbs, berries)Water, pools (chlorine resistant)
TreatmentTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazoleNitazoxanide (mainly if immunocompromised)
why: Smaller oocysts and nitazoxanide describe Cryptosporidium itself, not the organism in this outbreak.
Chlorine resistance and pool outbreaks are Cryptosporidium features, and this outbreak came from produce.
Tiny fungal spores treated with albendazole are microsporidia, not acid-fast oocysts of 8 to 10 micrometers.
Flagellated trophozoites treated with tinidazole describe Giardia, which is not acid-fast.
explain.takeaway: Cyclospora (8 to 10 micrometer acid-fast oocysts, fresh produce, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is distinguished from Cryptosporidium (4 to 7 micrometers, pools, nitazoxanide) by size and treatment.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Identify Cyclospora in a produce-linked diarrheal outbreak and distinguish it from other intestinal protozoa.

rows.why: Smaller oocysts and nitazoxanide describe Cryptosporidium itself, not the organism in this outbreak.
rows.if_right: 4 to 7 micrometer acid-fast oocysts in a swimming pool outbreak

rows.why: Chlorine resistance and pool outbreaks are Cryptosporidium features, and this outbreak came from produce.
rows.if_right: diarrhea traced to a chlorinated swimming pool

rows.why: Tiny fungal spores treated with albendazole are microsporidia, not acid-fast oocysts of 8 to 10 micrometers.
rows.if_right: very small spores in an immunocompromised patient with chronic diarrhea

rows.why: Flagellated trophozoites treated with tinidazole describe Giardia, which is not acid-fast.
rows.if_right: greasy, foul diarrhea after drinking stream water, with flagellated trophozoites

questions.stem:
A 25-year-old man returned 1 week ago from 4 weeks of hiking in Tanzania. On the last 2 days of the trip he ate raw salads from a farm that fertilized its fields with human waste. He wore hiking boots the whole time, though a fellow hiker who often walked barefoot was later diagnosed with Strongyloides. Three days ago he developed wheezing and a dry cough; he has never had asthma. Chest x-ray shows patchy infiltrates that change location over 2 days. Leukocytes are 11,500/microL (4,500 to 11,000) with 20% eosinophils (1 to 4). Three stool ova and parasite examinations collected on separate days are all negative.

Which of the following best explains the negative stool examinations at this point?
choices: Its eggs are laid on the perianal skin at night instead of in the stool
Larvae are still in the lungs and have not yet matured into adults in the gut
Eggs are trapped in tissue granulomas and cannot reach the intestinal lumen
Three samples are too few, because larvae are shed in stool only intermittently
Humans are incidental hosts, so this worm never lays eggs in the human gut

explain.html:
Several intestinal nematodes pass through the lungs before they reach the gut. Ascaris enters as swallowed eggs and travels gut, liver, lungs, gut; hookworm and Strongyloides enter through the skin and travel skin, lungs, gut. When larvae reach the lungs, a few days to a week after infection, they cause Loeffler syndrome: wheezing, dry cough, transient infiltrates and eosinophilia. Only after the larvae are coughed up, swallowed and mature into adults in the intestine do eggs or larvae appear in stool.

This traveler swallowed Ascaris eggs on salad grown in human waste; he wore boots, so his partner's Strongyloides, a skin-penetrating worm, is not his infection. His "asthma" about a week after exposure means the larvae are still in the lung phase, so three negative stool examinations reflect timing, not a poor test or a dead-end host. Repeating stool studies later, once adults are established, is what would show the organism.
explain.table:
WormEntryRouteStool O&P
AscarisSwallowed eggsGut, liver, lungs, gutEggs once adults are in the gut
Hookworm, StrongyloidesLarvae through skinSkin, lungs, gutEggs (hookworm) or larvae (Strongyloides, poor sensitivity) once in the gut
Angiostrongylus, ToxocaraSwallowed larvae or eggsLarvae stuck in tissue (incidental host)Never helpful
PinwormSwallowed eggsGut onlyUnhelpful; eggs on perianal skin
why: Perianal egg laying is pinworm, which has no lung phase and does not cause wheezing with shifting infiltrates.
Eggs trapped in tissue granulomas describe schistosomiasis, which presents with hematuria, not a migrating eosinophilic pneumonitis this early.
Poor stool sensitivity applies to Strongyloides, which enters through bare skin; he wore boots, his exposure was eggs on salad, and the problem is timing, not sampling.
Incidental hosts (Toxocara, Angiostrongylus) never grow adults; this worm passes through the lungs on its way to the gut, where it will become an adult.
explain.takeaway: During Loeffler syndrome (larval lung migration of Ascaris, hookworm or Strongyloides), stool O&P is negative because adults have not yet reached the intestine to produce eggs or larvae.
explain.topic: Loeffler syndrome comes before eggs in the stool
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Use the life cycle of an intestinal nematode to explain its lung phase and when stool testing becomes positive.

rows.why: Perianal egg laying is pinworm, which has no lung phase and does not cause wheezing with shifting infiltrates.
rows.if_right: a child with nocturnal perianal itching and no respiratory symptoms

rows.why: Eggs trapped in tissue granulomas describe schistosomiasis, which presents with hematuria, not a migrating eosinophilic pneumonitis this early.
rows.if_right: painless hematuria in someone who swam in an African freshwater lake

rows.why: Poor stool sensitivity applies to Strongyloides, which enters through bare skin; he wore boots, his exposure was eggs on salad, and the problem is timing, not sampling.
rows.if_right: a patient weeks to months into a chronic infection with only one stool sample sent

rows.why: Incidental hosts (Toxocara, Angiostrongylus) never grow adults; this worm passes through the lungs on its way to the gut, where it will become an adult.
rows.if_right: a child with fever, hepatomegaly and eosinophilia after eating soil where puppies play, or eosinophilic meningitis after eating snails
